text:
thyssenkrupp Uhde has secured pre-Front-End Engineering Design (pre-FEED) contracts from Fuella AS for the development of two large-scale green ammonia facilities in Brazil. The projects, named the Pecém Green Ammonia Project (PeGA) and the Açu Green Ammonia Project (AçuGA), represent significant steps toward establishing Brazil as a major producer and exporter of renewable ammonia. Located at the strategically important Ports of Pecém and Açu, the two facilities are each designed to produce approximately 400,000 tonnes of green ammonia annually using renewable energy sources.

The award of the pre-FEED contracts marks an important milestone in the advancement of both projects. During this phase, thyssenkrupp Uhde will focus on refining and optimizing the technical concepts, conducting critical engineering studies, and strengthening the commercial viability of the projects. The objective is to develop a solid technical and economic foundation that will support future investment decisions and facilitate the progression toward construction and operation.

The engineering work will leverage thyssenkrupp Uhde’s proprietary uhde® ammonia synthesis technology, which has been specifically developed to address the unique challenges associated with renewable-powered ammonia production. Unlike conventional ammonia plants that operate under steady energy supply conditions, green ammonia facilities rely on renewable electricity sources such as wind and solar power, which can fluctuate depending on weather conditions. The company’s technology is designed to efficiently manage these dynamic operating environments while maintaining reliable production performance.

In addition to supplying the ammonia synthesis technology, thyssenkrupp Uhde will provide comprehensive integration engineering services across the entire production chain. This includes the integration of electrolysis systems used to generate green hydrogen, balance-of-plant infrastructure, utilities, storage systems, and ammonia export and offloading facilities. By overseeing the integration of these interconnected components, the company aims to ensure efficient plant performance, operational reliability, and optimized project economics.

The PeGA and AçuGA developments are expected to play a key role in supporting the global energy transition. Green ammonia is increasingly viewed as an important low-carbon energy carrier and a sustainable alternative for industries seeking to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Beyond its traditional use in fertilizer production, green ammonia is gaining attention as a potential fuel for maritime transport, power generation, and hydrogen storage applications.

Nadja Håkansson, Chief Executive Officer of thyssenkrupp Uhde and Chief Operating Officer of thyssenkrupp Decarbon Technologies, emphasized the significance of the collaboration. She noted that the partnership combines thyssenkrupp Uhde’s extensive experience in ammonia technology with Fuella’s ambition to establish large-scale renewable ammonia hubs in Brazil. According to her, the projects demonstrate a shared commitment to accelerating the global transition toward cleaner energy systems and creating sustainable solutions for future ammonia markets.

Fuella AS Managing Director Dr. Thorsten Helms also expressed confidence in the partnership, highlighting thyssenkrupp Uhde’s technical expertise, understanding of local market conditions, and collaborative approach. He stated that these strengths were key factors in Fuella’s decision to select the company for its first Brazilian green ammonia developments.

As the projects move through the pre-FEED stage, both companies aim to advance commercial milestones, refine execution strategies, and prepare for subsequent development phases. If successfully implemented, the Pecém and Açu facilities could become major green ammonia production centers, supporting Brazil’s growing role in the global renewable energy and sustainable fuels market.

name: IMO & Shipping
title: From concept to reality: Exmar takes delivery of first ammonia-fuelled gas carrier
description:
Ammonia propulsion Propulsion power is supplied by a two-stroke, slow-speed ammonia dual-fuel WinGD X52DF-A-1.0 engine.
WinGD reports that it has secured orders for 40 X-DF-A engines for gas carriers, bulkers, tankers, and container ships.
The regulatory framework for using ammonia as fuel on gas carriers is still evolving, but it is becoming clearer.
Antwerpen and Arlon are the first two of four ammonia dual-fuel gas carriers for Exmar.
As the first ammonia-fuelled oceangoing vessels to enter operation, the operational experience from these Exmar midsize gas carriers will play a key role in further shaping and refining future regulations.
text:
Ammonia propulsion

Propulsion power is supplied by a two-stroke, slow-speed ammonia dual-fuel WinGD X52DF-A-1.0 engine. WinGD’s X-DF-A engine operates on a high-pressure ammonia-injection cycle and is equipped with selective catalytic reduction (SCR) technology to carefully manage nitrogen oxide (NOx) and nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions produced during combustion. Both NOx and N2O are powerful greenhouse gases.

As ammonia does not ignite easily, it requires about 5% pilot fuel in ammonia mode at 100% load.

The Swiss engine designer maintains that the engine’s performance in both ammonia and diesel modes is comparable to its established diesel-fuelled X-engine range. This was further confirmed during sea trials of Antwerpen in South Korea.

But after years of research and testing, WinGD is confident its first high-pressure dual fuel engine is the right platform to support owners who choose ammonia as their decarbonisation path.

WinGD reports that it has secured orders for 40 X-DF-A engines for gas carriers, bulkers, tankers, and container ships.

“By bringing together expertise from across the maritime value chain, we have demonstrated that ammonia propulsion can move from concept to commercial reality through safe, reliable, and fully automated engine technology,” said WinGD vice president R&D, Sebastian Hensel.

Mr Hensel’s colleague, Sotiris Topaloglou, global head of Testing & Validation, observed that 2026 “has been a year of milestones for ammonia as a next-generation marine fuel,” noting that factory and type acceptance testing for the company’s X-DF-A engine and sea trials for Antwerpen occurred this year. He said, “This follows many years of research, extensive testing, and rigorous validation to overcome all the technical challenges and deliver a propulsion solution that is not only safe but delivers the emissions cuts this industry needs to meet its 2050 net zero target.”

Added Mr Hensel, “With this engine, we’re offering shipowners real choice when it comes to investing in the fleet of the future: a safe and efficient dual-fuel engine that ensures compliance with today’s regulatory rules while being fully ready to meet the tighter emissions limits of tomorrow”.

Operating on blue or green ammonia will help mitigate carbon taxes under the EU Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime regulations. The owner notes that maritime penalties can be reduced and even avoided by sailing on blue and green ammonia, and will lower the ship’s Carbon Intensity Index as ammonia is carbon-free.

“Using clean ammonia as fuel can also positively impact the carbon intensity of the cargo,” said Exmar. “When the ammonia cargo is intended to qualify as Renewable Fuels of Non-Biological Origin (RFNBO) under the European Union Renewable Energy Directive (EU RED), its overall lifecycle emissions must remain below approximately 28 gCO₂eq per MJ. In this context, using clean ammonia as fuel provides a significant advantage in meeting this requirement.”

When transporting ammonia, Antwerpen will be able to use a portion of the cargo as fuel.

When carrying LPG, the ship will be bunkered via the cargo manifold. The vessel is designed to allow a smooth bunker operation of the deck tanks, maintaining full segregation from the cargo.

Ammonia will be used during oceangoing operations. At below 25% engine loads, such as during manoeuvring or cargo operations in port, the vessel will switch to compliant fuel.

Regulatory landscape evolves

While Exmar has been operating in the ammonia trades for more than 40 years, the Antwerp-based gas shipowner and infrastructure developer has broken new ground with the use of ammonia as fuel in shipping. The regulatory framework for using ammonia as fuel on gas carriers is still evolving, but it is becoming clearer. At the start of the project, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) IGC Code (section 16.9.2) did not permit the use of ammonia as fuel. But amendments to the IGC Code were approved and adopted at MSC 109, enabling the use of ammonia as fuel on ammonia carriers by July 2026.

In May, new safety guidelines for the use of ammonia as fuel on gas carriers were approved at the 111th Session of IMO’s Maritime Safety Committee (MSC 111), providing a clearer path for the commercial operation of ammonia-fuelled ships. The interim guidelines provide a practical framework to manage the safety risks associated with ammonia as a fuel, complementing Chapter 16 of the IGC Code, and allow the use of cargo as fuel on gas carriers.

The guidelines were developed through collaboration between Exmar, class society Lloyd’s Register (LR), and the Belgian Federal Public Service Mobility and Transport (FPS Mobility).

Antwerpen and Arlon are the first two of four ammonia dual-fuel gas carriers for Exmar. HD HHI will deliver the third in the series later this year and the fourth in early 2027. Named after Belgian cities that start with the letter “A”, all the vessels will be owned by Exmar LPG France. As the first ammonia-fuelled oceangoing vessels to enter operation, the operational experience from these Exmar midsize gas carriers will play a key role in further shaping and refining future regulations.

Marine fuel supplier Chimbusco Pan Nation (CPN) has completed the first B100 marine biofuel bunkering operation for an oil tanker in Hong Kong.

The fuel was delivered to TORM-operated tanker Torm Corrido on June 8, extending CPN's B100 bunkering service to another vessel segment, CPN said in a statement on its website on Wednesday.

description:
Belgian gas shipping company Exmar has completed construction of the first oceangoing vessel to be partly powered by an ammonia engine.
The ship, named MGC ANTWERPEN, is fitted with a dual-fuel engine, meaning it can also run on conventional diesel.
When operating on low-carbon ammonia, the ship produces virtually no emissions, delivering a reduction in greenhouse gases of up to 90 per cent compared to conventional vessels.
"We drew on our four decades of experience in transporting ammonia and other liquid gases," the company said.
"Thanks to extensive crew training and collaboration with the Belgian government, ammonia propulsion has now been realised and regulatory frameworks established for safe operations."
text:
Belgian gas shipping company Exmar has completed construction of the first oceangoing vessel to be partly powered by an ammonia engine. The Antwerp-headquartered company made the announcement on Wednesday.

The ship, named MGC ANTWERPEN, is fitted with a dual-fuel engine, meaning it can also run on conventional diesel. When operating on low-carbon ammonia, the ship produces virtually no emissions, delivering a reduction in greenhouse gases of up to 90 per cent compared to conventional vessels.

Exmar describes the milestone as "a very important step towards low-carbon shipping" and says it "places Exmar and its partners at the forefront of sustainable maritime innovation."

Safety hurdles remain

Ammonia propulsion is not without challenges. The substance is both highly toxic and explosive, requiring an extremely complex safety infrastructure. There are also concerns about nitrogen oxide emissions, raising the question of whether one pollutant is simply being replaced by another.

Exmar acknowledges these risks but says safety was central to the development process. "We drew on our four decades of experience in transporting ammonia and other liquid gases," the company said. "Thanks to extensive crew training and collaboration with the Belgian government, ammonia propulsion has now been realised and regulatory frameworks established for safe operations."

The MGC ANTWERPEN rolled off the production line in early April at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries in South Korea. Other partners in the project included WinGD, Nord Gas Solutions and Lloyd's Register. The consortium has described the vessel as "a historic milestone for shipping."

The project was developed through a collaboration between WinGD, EXMAR, engine builder HD Hyundai Engine & Machinery Division and shipbuilder HD Hyundai Heavy Industries.

The delivery comes as the maritime industry intensifies efforts to identify scalable low- and zero-carbon fuels capable of meeting increasingly stringent emissions regulations and the International Maritime Organization’s net-zero ambitions.

“We are proud to be part of delivering the world’s first ammonia-fuelled ocean-going vessel, a landmark achievement made possible through an intensive and highly collaborative development effort,” said Sebastian Hensel, Vice President of Research and Development at WinGD.

Ammonia has emerged as one of the leading candidates for decarbonizing deep-sea shipping because it contains no carbon and therefore produces no carbon dioxide emissions at the point of combustion. However, the fuel presents significant technical and safety challenges due to its toxicity and handling requirements, prompting years of development work by engine manufacturers, shipbuilders and classification societies.

title: IMO treaty on hazardous cargo takes effect in 2027 | Freight News
description:
The shipping industry has just under 18 months to prepare for a new international liability regime covering hazardous cargo transported by sea.
The convention will apply to incidents involving more than 2 000 hazardous and noxious substances, including chemicals, LNG, LPG, fertilisers and industrial acids.
"This treaty will ensure that those affected by hazardous cargo incidents involving ships can access fair and timely compensation, while providing legal certainty for industry and governments."
The 2010 HNS Convention complements existing IMO liability and compensation regimes addressing oil pollution and hazardous shipwrecks, extending similar protection to damage involving other hazardous and noxious substances.
The convention covers loss of life, personal injury, property damage, economic loss, clean-up costs and environmental damage arising from incidents involving hazardous and noxious substances carried by sea.
text:
The shipping industry has just under 18 months to prepare for a new international liability regime covering hazardous cargo transported by sea.

The International Convention on Liability and Compensation for Damage in Connection with the Carriage of Hazardous and Noxious Substances by Sea (2010 HNS Convention) will enter into force on November 29, 2027, after the conditions required for its implementation were met on May 29, according to the International Maritime Organization (IMO). The convention will apply to incidents involving more than 2 000 hazardous and noxious substances, including chemicals, LNG, LPG, fertilisers and industrial acids.

"The fulfilment of the conditions for the entry into force of the HNS Protocol is a long-awaited milestone that closes an important gap in the international liability and compensation regime for shipping," said IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez.

"This treaty will ensure that those affected by hazardous cargo incidents involving ships can access fair and timely compensation, while providing legal certainty for industry and governments."

The 2010 HNS Convention complements existing IMO liability and compensation regimes addressing oil pollution and hazardous shipwrecks, extending similar protection to damage involving other hazardous and noxious substances.

The convention covers loss of life, personal injury, property damage, economic loss, clean-up costs and environmental damage arising from incidents involving hazardous and noxious substances carried by sea.

How it will work

The convention applies the 'polluter pays' principle by ensuring that the shipping and hazardous and noxious substances (HNS) industries provide compensation for those who suffer loss or damage resulting from an HNS incident.

Shipowners will be held strictly liable, up to the maximum limit established under the convention, for costs arising from an HNS incident and will be required to maintain state-certified insurance or other financial security.

If damages exceed the shipowner's liability limit, additional compensation will be available through an HNS fund, financed through contributions paid post-incident by receivers of HNS cargo in contracting states.

It is estimated that approximately 65 000 ships will require HNS certificates of insurance or other financial security. The HNS fund will be administered by states, with contributions based on the actual compensation required.

Entry into force

There are currently 12 contracting states to the 2010 HNS Protocol, including South Africa, following ratifications by Belgium, Germany, the Kingdom of the Netherlands and Sweden in April 2026. The other contracting states are Canada, Denmark, Estonia, France, Norway, Slovakia and Türkiye.

Nine of the contracting states represent more than two million units of gross tonnage. Reports on contributing cargo submitted in accordance with Article 20 of the protocol confirmed that the required aggregate quantity of contributing cargo – more than 40 million tonnes – was achieved for the 2025 reporting year.

title: The member states approve the Conclusions on the EU Port Strategy | El Estrecho Digital
description:
The member states remind that maritime trade operates in a global environment and that European ports compete with facilities located in third countries.
The member states indicate that the application of the Port Strategy must be aligned with work on military mobility and with activities carried out within NATO.
The member states call for improving access to European funds through greater transparency, enhanced coordination, and simplified procedures.
Furthermore, the future strategy will be applied to a network made up of 283 maritime ports and 223 inland ports integrated into the trans-European transport network.
With these Conclusions, the member states set a common position to organize the upcoming community initiatives in an area considered essential for the economy, security, energy, and European connectivity.
text:
The member states of the European Union have adopted Council Conclusions on the EU Port Strategy, a document that reaffirms the role of ports as strategic assets for European autonomy, the security of supply chains, energy transition, and Europe's position in international maritime transport. The text has been approved within the framework of the Transport Council and establishes the main political guidelines for the development of the future community port strategy.

The initiative stems from the Communication presented by the European Commission on March 4, 2026, which proposed an EU Port Strategy aimed at improving the competitiveness, resilience, security, and sustainability of European ports. The approach covers both maritime and inland ports and is based on the community port policy of 2013, although adapted to a context marked by geopolitical, economic, technological, and environmental changes.

The Minister of Transport, Communications and Public Works of Cyprus, Alexis Vafeades, has stated that European ports are "much more than gateways for trade" and has defined them as strategic assets for the economy, security, and energy supply. He indicated that the Conclusions convey the need for competitive, resilient ports that are prepared for future challenges, through actions in security, energy transition, innovation, and investment.

The Council emphasizes that ports have become multifunctional industrial centers, while maintaining their traditional role as nodes of trade, mobility, and energy. This transformation requires expanding capacities, decarbonizing operations, digitizing processes, and improving safety levels, while respecting the national, regional, and local particularities of the different European port models.

One of the main axes of the document is competitiveness. The member states remind that maritime trade operates in a global environment and that European ports compete with facilities located in third countries. Therefore, they call for addressing the distortions arising from regulatory asymmetries, unfair competitive practices, and certain behaviors of non-community countries. They also request that efforts be made to ensure fair access conditions to the market for European operators in the port markets of third countries, in balanced and non-discriminatory terms.

The Conclusions also address the evaluation of foreign investments in European ports. The Council welcomes the Commission's intention to develop guidelines in this area, although it insists that EU ports must continue to be attractive destinations for investment. The member states believe that investment control must be based on risk criteria, proportionality, and non-discrimination, with special attention to economic security and the prevention of undue control over critical port infrastructure and operations.

Security and resilience occupy another central section of the text. The Council warns that ports face a more complex threat environment, which includes terrorism, sabotage, organized crime, corruption, cyberattacks, hybrid threats, and risks associated with the use of drones. In this context, the member states support both present and future initiatives aimed at protecting port infrastructure, including the European Ports Alliance, cooperation with international partners and third countries, and the future proposal of a community framework that facilitates cooperation among member states regarding background checks of port workers.

The document also places importance on military mobility. Ports are considered essential nodes for the movement of military personnel and equipment, thus linking their role directly to European defense preparedness. The member states indicate that the application of the Port Strategy must be aligned with work on military mobility and with activities carried out within NATO.

In energy matters, the Council recognizes the role of ports as key centers for the European energy transition. The Conclusions call for greater support for electricity supply in port, smart grids, electrification, and network integration, as long as investments are economically viable and respond to actual demand. The member states also consider it necessary to expedite the deployment of networks, the procedures for granting permits, and investments in clean energy technologies.

The text encourages the use of revenues from the EU emissions trading system to support maritime decarbonization throughout the entire value chain, including maritime transport, port infrastructure, and alternative fuels. At the same time, the Council acknowledges the existing concern about the effects of the EU ETS and other climate legislation on the competitiveness of European ports, particularly due to the risks of traffic diversion, carbon leakage, and relocation of investments. Therefore, it invites the Commission to continue monitoring these effects and to propose specific corrective measures when necessary, without deviating from the Union's climate objectives or the coordination with international frameworks.

Financing constitutes another priority of the document. The member states call for improving access to European funds through greater transparency, enhanced coordination, and simplified procedures. They also indicate that financing mechanisms should avoid unnecessary administrative burdens and remain neutral with respect to governance structures, concession models, and operational agreements of ports.

The Council also incorporates a social dimension into the port debate. The Conclusions recognize the contribution of ports to economic development, resilience, and territorial cohesion, especially in island, remote, outermost, and coastal regions. In this area, the importance of ensuring safe working conditions and investing in training, education, and professional development to accompany the technological transformation of the sector is highlighted. There is also a need to attract women and young people to maritime and port careers.

According to the data collected in the document, ports manage around 74% of the goods that enter or leave the European Union and about 395 million passengers each year. Furthermore, the future strategy will be applied to a network made up of 283 maritime ports and 223 inland ports integrated into the trans-European transport network. With these Conclusions, the member states set a common position to organize the upcoming community initiatives in an area considered essential for the economy, security, energy, and European connectivity.

title: MAMII calls for faster deployment of methane abatement tech in shipping - SAFETY4SEA
description:
Technology ready, but policy lagging A central point made by MAMII is that methane abatement technology is already commercially available and improving rapidly.
Industrial opportunity for Europe The report frames methane abatement not only as a climate necessity but also as an industrial opportunity for Europe.
Methane abatement is not just a climate issue – it is an industrial and economic opportunity for the EU.
Strategic implications for EU maritime policy Overall, MAMII argues that methane abatement offers a rare “win-win-win” pathway: faster emissions reductions, lower long-term costs, and stronger industrial leadership.
“The choice is clear,” the report highlights, “Methane abatement should be treated not as a niche issue, but as a strategic pillar of EU industrial and climate policy.”
text:
A new report published by the Methane Abatement in Maritime Innovation Initiative (MAMII) is calling on the European Union to elevate methane reduction from a technical concern to a core pillar of industrial and climate policy.

The report, titled “Turning methane abatement into a competitive advantage: A five-point action plan for the EU” and released in June 2026, sets out a five-point action plan urging EU policymakers to accelerate deployment of methane abatement technologies in shipping, particularly in the growing fleet of LNG-fueled vessels, where methane slip remains a significant emissions challenge.

Methane slip is the unburned fuel that is not fully combusted in ships’ engines. Although methane slip accounts for a generally a small percentage of the fuel used, in operations that use a significant amount of energy, methane slip can be a major source of emissions.

Five-point EU action plan

The report outlines five key recommendations for the EU:

#1 Recognize methane abatement as a strategic priority

Explicitly integrate methane abatement into key EU frameworks, including the implementation and delivery of the European Industrial Maritime Strategy (EIMS) and the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). Formal recognition is essential to create demand signals, unlock investment, and prevent methane from being overlooked or undervalued within broader decarbonization policies.

#2 Enable the use of verified, real-world emissions data

Build on the latest European Commission guidelines under FuelEU Maritime and clarify remaining implementation uncertainties, thereby enabling the widespread use of measurement-based methane emissions data. Over time, develop a dual-track approach that maintains the use of representative default emission factors while enabling and rewarding the voluntary use of verified, measurement-based emissions data where available.

#3 Scale investment and financial support for methane abatement technologies

Unlock funding and investment for methane abatement technologies by ensuring their explicit eligibility and prioritization across EU funding instruments, including the Net-Zero Industry Act, the Innovation Fund, and future competitiveness funding under the Industrial Accelerator Act and the next Multiannual Financial Framework. Key action points and policy asks: this should be complemented by a dedicated package of targeted financial incentives – such as grants, subsidies, tax credits, and access to affordable finance to accelerate early deployment. A portion of EU ETS revenues used to de-risk investments and support first movers.

#4 Build a shared evidence base through large-scale collaboration

Support and formalize a multi-stakeholder platform for large-scale trials, certification and data sharing, building on existing initiatives. This will accelerate technology validation, reduce adoption risks, and facilitate cross-industry learning in a fragmented sector.

#5 Use EU’s experience on methane standards to pave the way for global standards

Leverage EU data, regulatory experience and industrial expertise to shape global methane measurement and abatement standards at the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) level.

Methane seen as fast, high-impact climate lever

According to the publication, methane is the second-largest driver of global warming after CO₂ and is far more potent in the near term. Shipping emissions linked to LNG propulsion are likely to rise as the global dual-fuel fleet expands, with over 1,700 vessels already in operation and hundreds more on order.

This trend makes methane reduction an immediate priority rather than a future concern, especially as LNG continues to play a transitional role in global shipping.

Technology ready, but policy lagging

A central point made by MAMII is that methane abatement technology is already commercially available and improving rapidly. Recent advances are achieving 60–70% reductions in methane slip from engine improvements, with emerging after-treatment systems expected to push reductions to 80–90%.

Despite this progress, the authors argue that uptake remains limited due to insufficient policy incentives and a lack of consistent regulatory recognition for verified, real-world emissions data.

“The primary barrier is not technology, but policy alignment,” the report states, calling for “smarter, technology-centric frameworks” to unlock deployment at scale.

Industrial opportunity for Europe

The report frames methane abatement not only as a climate necessity but also as an industrial opportunity for Europe. It argues that EU-based technology providers are already active in the sector and could become global exporters of methane measurement and control systems if supported by stronger policy signals. It also positions methane reduction as a way to manage rising compliance costs under EU climate policies while maintaining competitiveness in global shipping markets.

Methane abatement is not just a climate issue – it is an industrial and economic opportunity for the EU. With the right policy environment, the EU can cut emissions, protect competitiveness, reduce long-term costs, and position itself as the global leader in maritime methane solutions

… said Panos Mitrou, Chair of the Methane Abatement in Maritime Innovation Initiative (MAMII).

Strategic implications for EU maritime policy

Overall, MAMII argues that methane abatement offers a rare “win-win-win” pathway: faster emissions reductions, lower long-term costs, and stronger industrial leadership. However, the it warns that without coordinated action, the EU risks locking in higher emissions and missing a key industrial growth opportunity.

“The choice is clear,” the report highlights, “Methane abatement should be treated not as a niche issue, but as a strategic pillar of EU industrial and climate policy.”

text:
The International Association of Dry Cargo Shipowners (Intercargo) has released a statement claiming that the new regulation from the International Maritime Organization (IMO) to determine the Carbon Intensity Index (CII) of ships, “cannot be used to achieve the desired decarbonization goals under real operational conditions, as it would not provide equitable, transparent, and undistorted emission reductions.”

According to this new regulation, each ship will receive a different classification based on how it is operated, subject to the decisions of the charterer.

The Carbon Intensity Index has faced criticism in the maritime sector, as there are factors beyond the control of shipowners and vessels that can have a significant negative impact. Some of these factors include adverse weather conditions, travel distance, waiting times in port, port infrastructure, and the aforementioned decisions of charterers.

According to Intercargo, “when considering distances and waiting times in port, ships with longer routes may produce more emissions but have a better CII rating compared to ships that travel shorter distances and produce fewer emissions.” This is why the association does not believe that the CII in its current format will help achieve the desired decarbonization goals. However, while it generally supports the short-term operational measure, “there are significant flaws that must be addressed in order to make the CII fit for its purpose,” it explains.

The association emphasizes that “the responsibility for decarbonization cannot rest solely on the shoulders of the ship operator. It is a challenge that must be addressed comprehensively by the entire maritime transport industry.”

Intercargo advocates for a fixed rate per ton of CO2 emitted from tank to wake (TtW) and subject to the outcome of ongoing discussions at the IMO regarding the Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) of fuel emissions. This rate would be combined with a reward system for avoided CO2 emissions for ships using “eligible alternative fuels.”

description:
The report includes an overview of maritime hydrogen systems, analyses of hydrogen-related accidents, identification of hydrogen hazards and risk mitigation measures, and relevant international regulations.
The report reviews recent developments in hydrogen fuel cell- and hydrogen internal combustion engine-powered vessels, along with hydrogen storage, supply, and fuel consumption systems.
The report examines major hazards associated with hydrogen-fueled ships, including hydrogen leakage and dispersion, fire and explosion, deflagration-to-detonation transition (DDT), jet fires, cryogenic hazards, and hydrogen embrittlement.
The report is intended to help stakeholders from industry, academia, and research institutions better understand and apply safety considerations for hydrogen-fueled ships.

text:
The Reliability Research Center of the Virtual Engineering Platform Research Division at the Korea Institute of Machinery & Materials participated as a key research partner in the publication of the report titled Safety Review of Hydrogen-Fueled Ships conducted in collaboration with the Korean Register, the report is a comprehensive technical document that systematically presents safety considerations, international regulations, and risk mitigation measures for hydrogen-fueled ships.

A research team led by Dr. Yongjin Kim, Head of the Reliability Research Center at KIMM, collaborated with Mr. Jun-Sung Park, General Manager at Korean Register, in preparing the report titled Safety Review of Hydrogen-Fueled Ships. The report includes an overview of maritime hydrogen systems, analyses of hydrogen-related accidents, identification of hydrogen hazards and risk mitigation measures, and relevant international regulations. Published in both Korean and English, the report is available for viewing and download on the Korean Register website(https://www.krs.co.kr/eng/).

Hydrogen is attracting attention as a promising alternative fuel for decarbonizing the maritime sector because it produces no carbon emissions during use and can serve as a feedstock for low-carbon fuels such as methanol. However, safe onboard use requires hydrogen to be stored either as compressed gas at high pressure or as liquid hydrogen at approximately -253°C. The report reviews recent developments in hydrogen fuel cell- and hydrogen internal combustion engine-powered vessels, along with hydrogen storage, supply, and fuel consumption systems.

Hydrogen has safety characteristics that differ from conventional fuels such as LNG due to its wide flammability range and extremely low minimum ignition energy. According to the Hydrogen Incidents and Accidents Database (HIAD 2.1), more than 66% of recorded hydrogen-related incidents resulted in fires or explosions. The report examines major hazards associated with hydrogen-fueled ships, including hydrogen leakage and dispersion, fire and explosion, deflagration-to-detonation transition (DDT), jet fires, cryogenic hazards, and hydrogen embrittlement. It further compares these risks with the International Code of Safety for Ships using Gases or Other Low-Flashpoint Fuels (IGF Code) to highlight safety considerations unique to hydrogen-fueled vessels.

Based on the interim safety guidelines for hydrogen-fueled ships currently being developed by the International Maritime Organization(IMO), the report explains the physical and chemical properties of hydrogen and key technical considerations for its safe use onboard ships. It presents practical risk mitigation measures for ship design and operation, including leak prevention, ventilation and inerting systems, material selection and compatibility, hazardous area classification, and gas and fire detection and suppression systems. The report is intended to help stakeholders from industry, academia, and research institutions better understand and apply safety considerations for hydrogen-fueled ships.

The IMO’s Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers(CCC) developed interim guidelines for hydrogen-fueled ships during its 11th session, and the guidelines are expected to receive final approval at the 111th session of the Maritime Safety Committee(MSC) in May 2026. As international hydrogen transportation and trade continue to expand, demand for hydrogen carriers and hydrogen-fueled ships is expected to increase. Published ahead of the adoption of the international guidelines, the report is expected to serve as a valuable technical reference for industry stakeholders.

Dr. Yongjin Kim emphasized, “This report systematically presents key hazards and risk mitigation measures for hydrogen-fueled ships and represents a meaningful outcome of collaboration among industry, academia, and research institutions. KIMM’s expertise in cryogenic and hydrogen embrittlement testing helped enhance the reliability and practical value of the report.” He added, “We will continue to support the advancement of Korea’s shipbuilding and maritime industries through safety standards development and material suitability evaluation for environmentally friendly vessels.”

Currently, SECA zones include the North Sea, the Baltic Sea, and most of the coasts of the U.S. and Canada.

text:
The Union of Greek Shipowners has reached out to Liberia and Japan to work on alternative proposals to the International Maritime Organization’s Net-Zero Framework, the group said June 5, also calling on the EU to make firmer commitments in rolling back its regulations on maritime greenhouse gas emissions.

After the UN agency’s member states voted to delay the framework’s adoption by a year in October 2025, Liberia and Japan have led proposals that would remove its mandatory GHG price mechanism in bids to seek consensus.

Speaking at a press conference, officials from UGS, Greece’s largest shipowners’ organization, said they would work with the countries to refine the regulatory proposals as the IMO is scheduled to have further discussions on the Net-Zero Framework later this year.

“Some parts of their proposals are positive, some parts are not feasible,” UGS President Melina Travlos. “We are in touch with them to hand over our own requests.”

In its current form, the NEF is designed to place a cost on maritime greenhouse gas emissions from later this decade to prompt a switch to low-carbon bunker fuels. Environmentalist groups and many shipping professionals have said a robust pricing mechanism is essential for the marine energy transition.

April’s delivered bunker price for 0.5%-sulfur fuel oil in Rotterdam was $17/Gigajoule, compared with $21/Gj for LNG and $35/Gj for bio-LNG, according to the Platts bunker cost calculator, which estimates bunker expenses based on Platts assessments. Platts is part of S&P Global Energy.

The Greek shipholders group has criticized that the framework in its current form is inappropriate, arguing that the lack of sustainable marine fuels could mean the IMO would simply be taxing ship operators in the form of the GHG cost while subsidizing developing countries and small island states.

Criticism against the EU

The EU officially supports the current framework, but Greece abstained from the IMO’s vote last October. Greece could face a greater risk of being taken to the European Court of Justice if expressing explicit opposition and presenting a new proposal, because it is bound by EU laws to act in a unified matter with other member states, according to UGC officials.

The UGC, meanwhile, has reiterated its call that the EU should phase out its Emissions Trading System for shipping and FuelEU Maritime rules on the GHG intensity of marine energy in EU-related trades should the IMO confirm a global regulation.

“ETS and FuelEU are hurting the European shipping industry’s competitiveness, but the EU didn’t say the ETS will be withdrawn once the IMO framework is in place,” Travlos said.

Greece is the largest shipowning country within the EU, with Greek-owned ships accounting for more than 19% of the global fleet, according to UGS figures. Last year, EU port calls accounted for 13.7% of the total for the Greek-owned fleet in deadweight tonnage.

The EU has stated it would review its regulations when the IMO finalizes the NZF to avoid double-counting, but how and when that happens remain uncertain. Brussels could stop implementing FuelEU, which has a similar design to the NZF, but it’s highly unlikely to exclude shipping from the ETS due to its contribution to national revenues, according to some bunker industry players.

John Lyras, a member of the UGS’ board of directors, said the ETS is a “sham” presented as an environmental measure as the EU collects the emission charges from international shipping but hasn’t used the proceeds to fund maritime decarbonization as promised.

Based on EU estimates of shipping GHG and current cargo prices, EU member states could generate over Eur7 billion ($8.2 billion) per year overall from ship operators. The European Commission has pledged to allocate Eur1.6 billion by 2030 to decarbonization projects. In March, the EU executive said it had provided Eur 600 million to shipping projects from the Innovation Fund since 2020.

Geopolitical tensions

UGS officials said Greek shipowners are not transporting sanctioned oil in the shadow fleet operations while expressing concerns that sanctions laws would create unfair competition.

“Greece is one of the world’s largest in owning ships, and after two or three sales sometimes Greek ships end up in the shadow fleet,” Travlos said. “Unfair targeting of Greek shipping needs to be stopped.”

In recent years, Greek tanker companies sold many aged tankers that would eventually become part of the shadow fleet and continued to participate in Russian oil trades as the EU approved such transactions under some conditions, including the compliance with the price cap regime.

In April, Brussels explicitly required EU-based tanker sellers to ensure their ships would not be used to transport Russian oil by the initial buyers and future buyers in resales in a sanctions package. But some industry participants, like Intertanko, said the new rules would be hard to enforce.

“EU sanctions are unilateral and not global. They distort market competition while we should protect fair competition,” Travlos said.

Greek tanker operators lifted nearly 687,000 b/d of Russian crude in April, the highest since October 2025, and nearly 17% of the total of Russia’s seaborne exports, according to data from S&P Global Commodities at Sea and Maritime Intelligence Risk Suite. This compared with 25% in November 2022, the month before the price cap took effect. UGS figures show Greek-owned ships account for 26% of the oil tanker fleet in deadweight tonnage.

Separately, Travlos said ships should be protected when transiting the Strait of Hormuz based on international laws for navigational freedom.

Iran has taken control of Hormuz, a choke point handling 20% of global oil and LNG flows in normal times, since its war with Israel and the US started Feb. 28 and limited ship traffic to 90% below the pre-war level. The IMO has recorded 40 maritime attacks during the conflict as of June 3, killing 11 seafarers.

Iranian officials have been seeking to formalize a toll system for Hormuz transits, but US officials have warned of sanction risks against whoever pays. Earlier this month, Evangelos Marinakis — whose companies control one of the largest Greek fleets — said in the TradeWinds Shipowners Forum that a fee might help resume cargo flows.

When asked to comment on Marinakis’s remarks, Travlos said: “Protecting shipping is super important … they shouldn’t put us on the spot for such discussions.”

Source: Platts

text:
International Maritime Organization urged its 176 member states and the global shipping industry to accelerate the implementation of measures aimed at protecting the marine environment as World Oceans Day was observed on June 8

IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez stressed the need to move beyond policymaking and focus on practical implementation of maritime environmental regulations

The organization highlighted key international conventions addressing marine pollution, invasive aquatic species, ship recycling, and ocean dumping

IMO reaffirmed its target of eliminating plastic waste discharges from ships into the sea by 2030 through its 2026 Strategy and Action Plan on Marine Plastic Litter

Member states agreed to develop a legally binding instrument to manage ships’ biofouling and curb the spread of invasive aquatic species

The trial phase for revised guidelines on reducing underwater radiated noise from ships was extended to 2028 to help protect marine biodiversity

The International Maritime Organization (IMO) has urged its 176 member states and the global shipping industry to accelerate the implementation of measures aimed at protecting the marine environment, emphasizing that effective enforcement is critical to safeguarding the world’s oceans.

IMO secretary-general Arsenio Dominguez called on governments and industry stakeholders to translate maritime environmental policies into concrete action.

“At IMO, we take our responsibility to protect the ocean seriously. With shipping being one of the main users of the ocean space, it is the reason why we focus on enhancing our regulatory framework to reduce pollution and address new challenges, such as underwater radiated noise and transboundary species,” Dominguez said in a video message for World Oceans Day, observed every June 8th.

“Beyond setting the rules, we must put policy into practice,” he added, referring to the IMO World Maritime Day theme for 2026-2027, “From Policy to Practice: Powering Maritime Excellence.”

Over the years, the IMO has developed a comprehensive regulatory framework aimed at preventing marine pollution, conserving biodiversity, and encouraging safer, more sustainable shipping practices globally.

Among the key international agreements are the MARPOL Convention, the Ballast Water Management Convention, the Anti-Fouling Systems Convention, the Hong Kong Convention, and the London Convention and Protocol, all of which are intended to safeguard marine ecosystems and reduce the environmental impact of shipping activities.

READ: IMO approves net-zero rules for shipping

The IMO also highlighted recent progress in addressing marine pollution, biodiversity protection, and climate-related challenges.

To combat marine plastic pollution, the organization adopted its 2026 Strategy and Action Plan to Address Marine Plastic Litter from Ships, reaffirming its goal of achieving zero plastic waste discharges from ships into the sea by 2030.

On biodiversity protection, member states agreed to develop a standalone legally binding instrument governing the control and management of ships’ biofouling, a key pathway for the transfer of invasive aquatic species across ecosystems.

The IMO further extended until 2028 the trial phase of its revised guidelines on reducing underwater radiated noise from shipping, with plans to commission a study that will help determine future regulatory measures aimed at minimizing adverse effects on marine life.

Meanwhile, discussions continue on measures to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from ships as the maritime sector seeks to align with global climate goals while maintaining the efficient movement of international trade.
